opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that there's a natural split between reasoning about the world and actually acting in it, and the architecture sort of mirrors that.

Gemini Robotics-ER, the "ER" being embodied reasoning, is really about taking the broad multimodal understanding that Gemini already has and sharpening it for the physical world. So things like spatial understanding: where are the objects, what's their 3D position, where would you grasp this mug, what's the trajectory to move something from here to there, how should I break this long task into steps. It's a very strong perception and planning model, and it can orchestrate. It can call tools, it can decide what the next subtask is, and it can check whether something succeeded.

Then the action model, the vision-language-action model, is the part that actually turns that intent into motor commands. It takes in the camera images and the instruction and outputs low-level actions at a high enough frequency that the robot moves smoothly and can react. That's a very different computational profile. You need low latency and you need it consistently, because a robot that's waiting on a network round trip in the middle of a grasp is a robot that drops things.

So the division of computation follows from those requirements. The big reasoning backbone is expensive, and it doesn't need to run at fifty hertz. Deciding "first open the drawer, then pick up the sponge" can tolerate some latency, so that can live in the cloud, where you have the big model and lots of compute. The part that closes the loop with the physical world has to be fast and reliable, so we put a lighter-weight action decoder on the robot itself. The backbone does the heavy lifting of understanding, and the on-device piece turns that into fast, reactive control. We also did work on fully on-device versions for settings where connectivity is a problem, and it's been encouraging how much capability you can retain there.

The bigger picture I'd emphasize is that this is roughly how people work too. You have a slower, deliberative layer that plans, and a faster layer that handles the actual movement without you consciously thinking about every joint angle. Getting those two to talk to each other well is a lot of the interesting research. How much the planner should specify, how much the action model should figure out on its own, and how they recover when something goes wrong. I don't think the boundary we have today is final. As models get more efficient, more of that reasoning will move onto the robot, and the split will keep shifting.

r001.rationale: It describes Gemini Robotics-ER as embodied reasoning for the physical world, but does not say it is a model variant specifically trained for those capabilities.

r002.rationale: It places the reasoning backbone in the cloud and a lighter-weight action decoder on the robot; it does not state that the action model itself is distributed across both.

r003.rationale: It does not address fine-tuning the action model from Gemini ER or whether Gemini ER must be invoked during robot actions.

r004.rationale: It says the boundary may shift as models become more efficient, but does not state that the cloud/local interface is configurable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that there are really two different kinds of thinking a robot has to do, and they live at pretty different timescales.

Gemini Robotics-ER, the embodied reasoning model, is sort of the slow, deliberate part. It's a VLM that we've trained to be really good at the spatial and physical understanding you need for robotics: pointing at objects, estimating 3D bounding boxes, predicting grasps, figuring out trajectories, and then doing the high-level reasoning, like "to make a sandwich, first I need to open the fridge, then take out the bread." It's also a safety layer in some sense, it can reason about whether an action is a good idea at all. That model is big, and it benefits from being big, so it makes a lot of sense to run it in the cloud. You can tolerate a few hundred milliseconds or even seconds of latency for that kind of reasoning because it's not what's closing the loop on your motors.

Then there's the action model, the VLA, which actually outputs the low-level motor commands. That has to run at something like tens of hertz, it has to be reactive to the world, and it can't be sitting there waiting on a network round trip. If someone bumps the table or an object slips, you need to respond immediately. So that part is where we put a lot of effort into distillation and getting a model small enough to run on-robot, which is what the on-device version of Gemini Robotics is about. And honestly, the surprising thing was how little we lost. You can get a lot of the generality and dexterity in a model that fits on the robot's own compute.

So the division of computation falls out pretty naturally from that. The cloud handles the "what should I be doing and why" at a coarse timescale, and the robot handles "how do I actually move my arm right now" at a fine timescale. The ER model can plan, decompose tasks, and call the action model as a kind of tool, and the action model just needs enough semantic understanding to interpret those sub-instructions and execute robustly.

There's also a practical reason this matters. People want robots that work when the Wi-Fi drops, or in environments where they can't send video to the cloud for privacy reasons. If the whole stack depended on connectivity, you'd have a robot that freezes every time there's a hiccup. So keeping the reactive layer local isn't just about latency, it's about reliability and trust.

Longer term, I think the boundary will keep moving. On-device compute is getting better, the models are getting more efficient, and ideally you'd want as much as possible running locally with the cloud there for the really hard reasoning or for learning across the whole fleet. But the architectural separation between reasoning and acting, I think that's going to stay useful regardless of where each piece physically runs.

r001.rationale: It describes Gemini Robotics-ER as an embodied reasoning model trained for robotics-specific spatial and physical understanding.

r002.rationale: It places the reactive action model on the robot and higher-level reasoning in the cloud, but does not say the action model itself is distributed across both.

r003.rationale: It says ER can plan and call the action model, but does not explain that fine-tuning the action model from ER does not require invoking ER during robot actions.

r004.rationale: It says the boundary may shift as on-device compute improves, but does not state that the cloud/local interface is configurable.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a division between reasoning about what needs to happen and generating the actions that make it happen. Gemini ER is the embodied reasoning side: understanding the scene, reasoning about spatial relationships, and breaking a task down into steps. The action model takes that context together with the robot’s observations and turns it into physical behavior.

That connects to the cloud-versus-robot question, but they’re slightly different divisions. You can benefit from more computation for higher-level reasoning, where you might need to interpret an ambiguous instruction or think through a multistep task. The execution loop has a different constraint: the robot needs to respond quickly as the world changes. If an object moves or a grasp doesn’t go as expected, you want that feedback handled close to the robot.

So the useful picture is a slower, more deliberative loop working with a fast, reactive loop. The important part is making those loops communicate well. Reasoning has to stay grounded in what the robot can actually do, and execution has to feed back what actually happened.

r002.rationale: It discusses cloud reasoning and robot-side execution, but does not state that the Gemini Robotics action model itself is distributed across both.

r003.rationale: It does not mention fine-tuning the action model from Gemini ER or clarify whether Gemini ER must be invoked during robot actions.

r004.rationale: It does not state that the interface between cloud and local robot computation is configurable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as separating reasoning about what to do from the control needed to actually do it. Gemini ER is the embodied reasoning side: understanding the scene, reasoning about spatial relationships, and breaking a task into steps. The action model takes the robot’s observations and an instruction and turns those into physical actions.

Those capabilities are complementary. You want the reasoning model to be grounded in what the robot can perceive and do, and you want the action model to benefit from that broader understanding without having to solve the entire task at every control step.

The cloud-versus-robot question is a related but separate design choice. The cloud gives you access to more computation for higher-level reasoning, while running on the robot helps with latency and connectivity, particularly for the tight perception-action loop. So the natural architecture is to use larger-scale reasoning when it’s useful and keep time-sensitive execution close to the hardware. Exactly where you draw that boundary depends on the task and the robot.
